pages.text: Bempong and Fiati held three dry bean seeds. “Are they alive?” asked Fiati. “They look like small stones.” Their teacher said, “A seed is alive, but it is asleep. Let us wake it up.”
sentences: Bempong and Fiati held three dry bean seeds.
“Are they alive?” asked Fiati.
“They look like small stones.” Their teacher said, “A seed is alive, but it is asleep.
Let us wake it up.”
pages.alt: Bempong and Fiati hold three dry brown bean seeds in their open palms while their smiling teacher stands beside them in a sunlit Ghanaian classroom.

pages.text: They soaked the seeds overnight. The next day, the seeds were soft and bigger. They put the seeds on a wet cloth inside a clear cup and put the cup in a warm place. Each day, they kept the cloth wet.
sentences: They soaked the seeds overnight.
The next day, the seeds were soft and bigger.
They put the seeds on a wet cloth inside a clear cup and put the cup in a warm place.
Each day, they kept the cloth wet.
pages.alt: Bempong and Fiati place plump, soaked bean seeds onto a folded wet white cloth inside a clear cup on a sunny wooden classroom windowsill.

pages.text: After a few days, the skin of one seed split open. A small white root came out and grew downwards. “The root comes first,” said Bempong. “It will take in water.”
sentences: After a few days, the skin of one seed split open.
A small white root came out and grew downwards.
“The root comes first,” said Bempong.
“It will take in water.”
pages.alt: Close view of the clear cup as Bempong points to a bean seed whose brown coat has split open with a small white root growing downwards.

pages.text: Soon, a green shoot grew upwards. It pushed up two small leaves. “The bean seed has two halves, and it opens into two seed leaves,” said the teacher. “A maize seed has one, so a maize plant starts as one green blade.”
sentences: Soon, a green shoot grew upwards.
It pushed up two small leaves.
“The bean seed has two halves, and it opens into two seed leaves,” said the teacher.
“A maize seed has one, so a maize plant starts as one green blade.”
pages.alt: Beside the teacher, two clear cups sit side by side: one showing a bean seedling with two rounded green leaves and one showing a maize seedling with a single upright green blade.

pages.text: The children drew the plant every two days in their notebooks. First: a soft seed. Next: a root. Next: a shoot. Last: green leaves. “A seed needs water, air and warmth to sprout,” said Fiati.
sentences: The children drew the plant every two days in their notebooks.
First: a soft seed.
Next: a root.
Next: a shoot.
Last: green leaves.
“A seed needs water, air and warmth to sprout,” said Fiati.
pages.alt: Fiati and Bempong sit at their wooden desk drawing four simple wordless pictures of a sprouting bean plant in an open sketchbook.

pages.text: They planted the seedlings in soil in the school garden and watered them gently. “Now they need light, too,” said Bempong. Fiati smiled. “The sleeping seed is awake. And we waited for it.”
sentences: They planted the seedlings in soil in the school garden and watered them gently.
“Now they need light, too,” said Bempong.
Fiati smiled.
“The sleeping seed is awake.
And we waited for it.”
pages.alt: In the sunlit school garden, Bempong and Fiati kneel beside dark soil planting their young green bean seedlings and watering them gently.

activities.question: Which part of the seed grew out first?
What does a seed need to sprout?

activities.prompt: Put the seed’s journey in order.

activities.definition: To start to grow from a seed.

glossary.definition: The small part of a plant that can grow into a new plant.
The part of a plant that grows down into the soil and takes in water.
The young part of a plant that grows upwards from a seed.
